items.stem: A good is scarce, in the economic sense, when

options.A: everyone already has as much as they want
options.B: more of it is wanted than is freely available at a zero price
options.C: it cannot be produced by labour

items.explanation: Scarcity means wants exceed availability at a zero price, so the good has an opportunity cost. A free good does not.

items.stem: A production possibility frontier shows

options.A: the prices consumers are willing to pay
options.B: only the goods that are imported
options.C: the maximum combinations of two goods that can be produced when resources are fully and efficiently employed
options.D: combinations that are always inside the country's budget

items.explanation: The PPF is a boundary of maximum output of two goods, given resources and technology, with full employment of those resources.

items.stem: Opportunity cost is

options.A: the sum of money spent on every alternative
options.B: a cost that is always zero in a mixed economy
options.C: the next best alternative given up when a choice is made
options.D: the total output of the economy

items.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the best forgone alternative, not every alternative added together.

items.stem: The three basic choices for an economy are

options.A: what to consume, how to save, and for whom to lend abroad only
options.B: what to tax, how to vote, and for whom to export only
options.C: what the central bank prints, how banks advertise, and for whom interest is paid
options.D: what to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce

items.explanation: Scarcity forces every economy to decide what is produced, which methods are used, and who receives the output.

items.stem: Which contrast between microeconomics and macroeconomics is correct?

options.A: Microeconomics studies inflation only; macroeconomics studies one firm only
options.B: Macroeconomics ignores national income and studies only one household
options.C: Microeconomics studies individual markets; macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole
options.D: Both study only the foreign-exchange market

items.explanation: Microeconomics looks at households, firms and particular markets. Macroeconomics looks at aggregates such as national income, inflation and unemployment.

items.stem: Which statement best defines economics as it is used in this syllabus?

options.A: The study of how banks set every price in a modern economy
options.B: The study of unlimited resources and limited human wants
options.C: The recording of government tax revenue only
options.D: The study of how scarce resources are allocated among competing uses

items.explanation: Economics starts from scarcity: wants exceed the resources available, so choice is unavoidable.

items.explanation: Points inside the frontier are attainable but inefficient. Points on the frontier are efficient. Points outside are unattainable with current resources.

items.stem: A point outside the current production possibility frontier is

options.B: proof that the economy is in recession
options.C: always preferred by consumers to a point on the frontier
options.D: unattainable with present resources and technology

items.explanation: The frontier is the maximum. Output beyond it needs more resources or better technology.

items.stem: The government of St Brice spends a given budget on a new clinic and therefore postpones a harbour repair. The opportunity cost of the clinic is

options.A: the wages of nurses in other countries
options.B: the sum of every project the government has ever discussed
options.C: zero, because the clinic is useful
options.D: the harbour repair that was given up

items.explanation: The opportunity cost of a choice is the next best alternative forgone, here the harbour repair.

items.stem: Which statement is normative?

options.A: Harbour Cay produced 20 000 tonnes of fish last year in this classroom example
options.B: The government of Harbour Cay ought to subsidise school meals
options.C: The marginal propensity to consume is the change in consumption divided by the change in income
options.D: A price ceiling set below equilibrium causes a shortage

items.explanation: A normative statement contains a value judgement such as 'ought'. The other statements are positive: they can be tested.

options.A: producers hold unwanted stocks that keep growing
options.C: the government fixes a price below the market-clearing price

items.explanation: Equilibrium is the price at which planned purchases equal planned sales, so there is no tendency for the price to change.

items.stem: A specific tax is levied on producers. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The tax shifts demand to the right
options.B: Buyers always pay the entire tax, whatever the elasticities
options.C: Sellers always pay the entire tax, whatever the elasticities
options.D: The price buyers pay rises and the price sellers keep falls, and the more inelastic side of the market bears more of the tax

items.explanation: The tax drives a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive. Incidence depends on relative elasticities: the less elastic side bears more.

options.A: no change, because a floor above equilibrium does not bind
options.D: an increase in quantity demanded above quantity supplied

items.explanation: A price floor above equilibrium is binding. At that higher price, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.

items.stem: A price ceiling is set below the equilibrium price. The result is

options.A: a quantity traded equal to quantity demanded
options.C: a shortage, and the quantity traded is the quantity supplied
options.D: no effect, because a ceiling below equilibrium is non-binding

items.explanation: A maximum price below equilibrium is binding. Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, and trade is limited by the smaller amount, which is quantity supplied.

items.stem: A limitation of cardinal marginal-utility theory is that

options.A: satisfaction cannot in practice be measured in objective utility units
options.B: it denies that consumers respond to prices
options.C: it assumes diminishing marginal utility, which no textbook uses
options.D: it cannot be stated as an equation

items.explanation: The cardinal approach treats utility as measurable in utils. In practice utility is not cardinally measurable, which is why the ordinal indifference-curve approach is used.

items.explanation: Marginal utility is the change in total utility from one extra unit. Total utility is the sum of satisfaction from all units.

items.stem: Which property of a standard indifference map is correct?

options.B: Curves further from the origin represent higher satisfaction, and two curves do not cross
options.C: Curves slope upwards because both goods are desirable
options.D: Curves cross at the consumer's equilibrium

items.explanation: More of both goods is preferred, so higher curves are better. Crossing would imply inconsistent rankings. Standard curves are convex to the origin.

items.stem: A consumer buys goods A and B. The marginal utility of A divided by its price is greater than the marginal utility of B divided by its price. To move toward equilibrium the consumer should

options.D: buy more of both in the same proportion

items.explanation: Equilibrium requires MUa/Pa = MUb/Pb. If MUa/Pa is higher, the last dollar spent on A yields more utility, so the consumer gains by switching spending toward A.

options.A: the same thing as supernormal profit
options.C: the minimum return that keeps the entrepreneur in the industry, and it counts as zero economic profit

items.explanation: Normal profit covers the opportunity cost of enterprise and is included in economic cost. Economic profit is then zero. Supernormal profit is positive economic profit.

items.stem: A Pigouvian tax on a negative production externality should, in principle, be set equal to

options.A: the entire price of the good
options.B: the marginal external cost at the socially efficient output
options.D: zero, because taxes cannot change output

items.explanation: A tax equal to marginal external cost makes the firm face marginal social cost, so it chooses the smaller socially efficient output.

items.stem: An argument against government intervention is that

options.A: administrative costs and political pressure can make the cure worse than the market failure

items.explanation: Intervention is not automatically better than the market. The benefits of a policy have to be compared with its costs and with the risk of government failure.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: Government failure occurs when

options.A: a Pigouvian tax equals marginal external cost
options.C: intervention leaves society worse off than the market outcome it tried to correct, or wastes resources

items.explanation: Governments can misjudge the size of an externality, favour interest groups, or impose administrative costs larger than the benefit.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: Regulation that simply bans pollution above a limit, compared with a tax,

options.A: can hit a quantity target but may not minimise the cost of doing so if firms face different abatement costs
options.B: is the same instrument as a producer subsidy
options.C: always costs less than a tax for every firm

items.explanation: A uniform quota ignores which firms can cut pollution more cheaply. A tax or permit market gives those firms a stronger reason to cut more.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: Tradable pollution permits

options.A: are a form of public good provided free to polluters with no cap
options.B: cap the total quantity of pollution and let firms buy and sell the right to emit
options.C: force every firm to emit the same amount whatever the cost
options.D: set no limit on total pollution

items.explanation: The cap fixes the total externality. Trade lets firms that can cut emissions cheaply sell permits to firms that cannot, which reduces the cost of meeting the cap.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.stem: A natural monopoly, with falling average cost over the whole market, is sometimes regulated rather than broken up because

options.A: one firm can produce the whole output at a lower average cost than several firms
options.B: competition always lowers average cost in this case
options.C: marginal cost is above average cost

items.explanation: When average cost is still falling at market demand, splitting the firm raises cost. Regulation may then be used to limit the monopoly price.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: A subsidy is a suitable market-based response to

options.A: a pure monopoly, if the aim is to raise price
options.B: a positive externality that causes under-consumption or under-production
options.C: a shortage caused by a price ceiling, if the aim is to lower supply
options.D: a negative externality that causes over-production, if the aim is to raise output further

items.explanation: A subsidy lowers the private cost or price and increases quantity, which can close the gap created by a positive externality.

items.stem: Competition policy is used to

options.A: force every industry to become a monopoly
options.B: ban all advertising of differentiated products
options.C: restrict abuse of monopoly power and anti-competitive agreements
options.D: set price equal to average fixed cost

items.explanation: Laws against cartels, mergers that harm competition, and abuse of a dominant position are meant to move price and output closer to the competitive outcome.

items.stem: Compulsory labelling of the health risk on a demerit good is an intervention aimed at
items.explanation: If over-consumption comes from consumers not knowing the risk, information can change demand without banning the good.

items.stem: Governments often provide street lighting directly because

options.A: it is a private good with no free riders
options.C: it is a public good and the market would under-provide it
options.D: marginal cost is always above willingness to pay

items.explanation: Non-excludability and non-rivalry make voluntary payment unreliable, so public provision or public finance is a standard remedy.

options.A: raise consumption toward the socially desirable level
options.C: turn the good into a demerit good

items.explanation: A zero price removes the private cost barrier. That can be justified when information failure or external benefits mean the market quantity is too low, though it has a cost in taxation and possible over-use.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: Which intervention directly targets a negative consumption externality of cigarettes?

options.A: A subsidy that lowers the price
options.B: A price ceiling that creates a shortage and raises consumption
options.C: A specific tax that raises the price buyers pay
options.D: Free provision of cigarettes as if they were a public good

items.explanation: A tax reduces quantity demanded. A subsidy or free provision would increase consumption, which is the wrong direction for a demerit good.

items.stem: Which is a possible cost of using a tax to correct an externality?

options.A: Taxes cannot be levied on producers
options.B: If the tax is much larger than the marginal external cost, output falls below the social optimum
options.C: The tax removes private costs as well as external costs from the firm's accounts
options.D: A correctly set tax always increases the externality

items.explanation: Too large a tax over-corrects. The firm then produces less than the output at which marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost.

items.stem: A demerit good is

options.C: a good that the free market over-consumes relative to the socially desirable level

items.explanation: Demerit goods, such as cigarettes in the usual example, are over-consumed because consumers ignore harm to themselves or others, or lack information.

items.stem: A merit good is

options.B: a good that the free market under-consumes relative to the socially desirable level, often because of poor information or a positive externality
options.D: a good that is always non-excludable

items.explanation: Merit goods, such as preventive health care or basic education in the usual examples, are under-consumed if left only to private decisions. They can still be private goods.

items.stem: A negative production externality means

options.A: the good is a public good
options.B: marginal social benefit is above marginal private benefit
options.C: marginal social cost is below marginal private cost, and the market produces too little
options.D: marginal social cost is above marginal private cost, and the free market produces too much

items.explanation: The firm ignores costs imposed on others, so MSC = MPC + external cost. Private equilibrium output is higher than the social optimum.

options.A: the good must be a demerit good
options.B: marginal social cost exceeds marginal private cost
options.D: marginal social benefit exceeds marginal private benefit, and the free market consumes too little

items.explanation: Others gain from this consumption, but the buyer counts only private benefit, so too little is consumed.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: A pure private good is

options.B: non-rival and excludable only if it is a public good

items.explanation: One person's consumption of a private good reduces what is left for others, and non-payers can be kept from using it.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: A pure public good is

options.D: excludable and always sold by a monopolist

items.explanation: Non-rival means one person's use does not reduce another's. Non-excludable means non-payers cannot be kept out. Street lighting is the usual example.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: An allocation is Pareto efficient when

options.A: nobody can be made better off without making someone else worse off
options.B: one person can gain without any cost to anyone else, and that change has not yet been made

items.explanation: Pareto efficiency means all mutually beneficial changes have already been exhausted. It does not mean incomes are equal.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: Information failure causes market failure when

options.A: the good is a free good
options.B: buyers or sellers lack information and so consume or produce the wrong amount

items.explanation: If consumers do not know the benefits of a merit good, or the harm of a demerit good, their choices are not the efficient ones.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: Market failure means that

options.A: the free market does not achieve an efficient allocation of resources
options.C: the market price is above zero

items.explanation: Failure is judged against efficiency, especially allocative efficiency, not against the mere existence of a price.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: Missing markets, as a cause of market failure, means

options.B: the stock exchange has closed for a holiday
options.D: some costs or benefits are not priced, so no market coordinates them

items.explanation: Externalities and public goods are examples of effects that lack a complete market. There is then no price to signal the right quantity.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: An open-access fishery, where anyone may fish and one boat's catch reduces the stock, is

options.A: rival but non-excludable, so it tends to be overused
options.B: a pure private good, because a licence is always required
options.C: a pure public good, because the fish are non-rival

items.explanation: Fish taken by one boat are not available to others, so the resource is rival. If nobody can be excluded, fishers ignore the cost they impose on others and overfish. That is not a pure public good.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: Education can be excludable and rival in a classroom, yet still be treated as a merit good. That shows

options.B: rivalry and exclusion are the same thing
options.C: education cannot have a positive externality
options.D: a merit good need not be a public good

items.explanation: Public goods are defined by non-rivalry and non-exclusion. Merit goods are defined by under-consumption. A good can be one without being the other.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: Monopoly power is a source of market failure because

options.A: price is set above marginal cost, so too little is produced
options.B: free entry removes every barrier at once
options.D: the firm must produce at minimum average cost

items.explanation: The output where MR = MC is smaller than the output where P = MC. That under-production is allocatively inefficient.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: Smoke from a factory harms nearby residents and the firm does not pay them. This is
items.explanation: The cost falls on third parties during production and is not in the firm's private cost. Output is likely to be too high.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: The free-rider problem of a public good arises because

options.A: the government always over-provides private goods
options.B: marginal cost is above average cost
options.C: people can benefit without paying, so the market under-provides the good
options.D: the good is rival, so one user blocks every other user

items.explanation: If exclusion is impossible, each person waits for someone else to pay. Private firms then cannot cover costs from voluntary payments.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: The socially efficient output of a good with an external cost is where

options.A: marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost
options.B: marginal private cost equals marginal private benefit, ignoring the external cost
options.C: price is below marginal social cost by as much as possible
options.D: output is zero in every case

items.explanation: Efficiency requires all benefits and costs, including external ones, to be balanced at the margin. The private market equates only private benefit and private cost.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: A firm is best described as

options.A: the whole group of firms selling a product
options.C: a unit that employs factors to produce goods or services for sale

items.explanation: A firm produces for sale. An industry is the group of firms producing a particular product.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: A four-firm concentration ratio of 90 percent means

options.B: each of four firms has a 90 percent share
options.C: the largest four firms supply 90 percent of the market

items.explanation: CR4 is the sum of the market shares of the four largest firms. A high ratio means the industry is concentrated.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: A limitation of concentration ratios is that they

options.B: do not by themselves show barriers to entry, contestability or how firms actually behave
options.D: prove that price equals marginal cost

items.explanation: A high share can still be consistent with competitive pressure if entry is easy. Concentration is a structural clue, not a full measure of performance.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: A market is contestable when

options.B: entry and exit are easy and sunk costs are low, so even a few firms may behave competitively
options.C: one firm owns an essential resource that cannot be duplicated

items.explanation: The threat of hit-and-run entry can discipline incumbents if leaving does not sacrifice large sunk costs.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker, so

options.A: marginal revenue is below average revenue
options.B: price equals average revenue and marginal revenue
options.C: the firm sets the market price on its own
options.D: average revenue falls as it sells more

items.explanation: The firm can sell any quantity at the market price, so the demand it faces is horizontal and P = AR = MR.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: A profit-maximising monopolist chooses the output where

options.A: marginal cost equals average revenue, always
options.C: price equals minimum average cost, by law
options.D: marginal revenue equals marginal cost, and then charges the price on the demand curve

items.explanation: The output rule is MR = MC for any profit-maximising firm. The monopolist reads the price from demand, so price exceeds marginal cost.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: A single-price monopoly is allocatively inefficient because

options.A: price is greater than marginal cost
options.C: it must produce at minimum average cost
options.D: it earns only normal profit by definition

items.explanation: P > MC means consumers value extra units more than they cost to produce, but the monopolist does not produce them.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: An industry is

options.A: the group of firms producing a particular type of good or service
options.B: the same thing as a household

items.explanation: Industry refers to the collection of firms in a market, not to one firm.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: Compared with the four-firm concentration ratio, the Herfindahl-Hirschman index

options.C: cannot be calculated from percentage shares
options.D: gives extra weight to firms with larger shares because shares are squared

items.explanation: Squaring means a market dominated by one firm has a higher HHI than a market whose four leaders are equal, even if CR4 is similar.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: For a single-price monopolist facing a downward-sloping demand curve,

options.B: marginal revenue equals average revenue at every output
options.C: the firm is a price taker
options.D: marginal revenue is below average revenue

items.explanation: To sell one more unit the monopolist lowers the price on all units, so the extra revenue is less than the price. MR lies below AR.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: In long-run equilibrium a perfectly competitive firm produces where

options.A: marginal cost is below average variable cost
options.B: price equals minimum average total cost, so profit is normal
options.D: price is above average total cost

items.explanation: Free entry drives price to the minimum of average total cost. The firm then earns normal profit and is productively efficient.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: In long-run monopolistic competition the firm

options.A: earns normal profit and has excess capacity, producing less than the output at minimum average cost
options.C: sets price equal to marginal cost
options.D: produces at the minimum of average cost

items.explanation: Entry shifts the firm's demand until it is tangent to average cost, which is normal profit. Tangency is on the falling part of average cost, so there is excess capacity, and price still exceeds marginal cost.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: In the kinked-demand model of oligopoly, price is rigid because

options.B: rivals are assumed to match a price cut but not a price rise
options.C: demand is perfectly elastic for a price cut

items.explanation: A price rise loses customers if rivals do not follow, while a price cut is matched so sales hardly rise. The kink creates a break in marginal revenue, and marginal cost can move inside that break without changing price.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: Long-run equilibrium in perfect competition is allocatively efficient because

options.B: price is greater than marginal cost
options.C: the firm holds spare capacity on purpose

items.explanation: Allocative efficiency requires P = MC, so the value consumers place on the last unit equals the cost of producing it. Perfect competition meets that condition.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: Market structure is distinguished by features such as

options.A: the number of firms, product similarity, ease of entry and information
options.B: whether the finance minister is elected
options.C: the month of the year only
options.D: the colour of the product only

items.explanation: Those four features are the usual basis for perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition and oligopoly.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: Monopolistic competition is characterised by

options.A: a homogeneous product and no advertising
options.D: many firms, differentiated products, and free entry

items.explanation: Product differentiation gives each firm some price-setting power, but free entry prevents long-run supernormal profit.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: Oligopoly is a market with

options.A: thousands of firms that ignore each other
options.B: free entry and a homogeneous product sold by price takers
options.D: a few firms, each aware that its decisions affect rivals

items.explanation: Interdependence is the defining conduct of oligopoly: each firm must consider how the others will react.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: Which features fit a pure monopoly?

options.A: Many sellers of differentiated products and free entry
options.B: Many sellers of an identical product and free entry
options.C: One seller, no close substitute, and barriers that block entry
options.D: A few firms that must each take the price as given

items.explanation: Monopoly is a single seller protected by barriers, so close substitutes and free entry are absent.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: Which set of features fits perfect competition?

options.A: One seller protected by barriers to entry
options.B: A few interdependent sellers of similar products
options.C: Many buyers and sellers, a homogeneous product, free entry and perfect information
options.D: Many sellers of differentiated products and free entry

items.explanation: Perfect competition requires price-taking firms selling an identical product, with no barriers to entry.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: A monopolist can earn supernormal profit in the long run if

options.B: barriers stop new firms from entering

items.explanation: Barriers protect supernormal profit. Free entry, as in perfect or monopolistic competition, competes that profit away in the long run.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: A perfectly competitive firm is making supernormal profit in the short run. With free entry, the long-run outcome is

options.A: entry of firms, a lower market price, and only normal profit
options.B: permanent supernormal profit because entry is blocked
options.D: exit of firms and a higher price

items.explanation: Supernormal profit attracts entry. Market supply rises, price falls, and profit is competed down to normal profit.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
items.stem: Members of a cartel have an incentive to cheat because

options.B: cheating always raises the market price
options.C: a cartel has no agreed output
options.D: a firm that secretly sells more at a price below the cartel price can raise its own profit

items.explanation: The cartel price is above marginal cost, so one firm gains by selling extra units if it is not detected. That incentive makes cartels unstable.

items.stem: A Gini coefficient of 0 means

options.B: that the country has no income
options.D: that the Lorenz curve cannot be drawn

items.explanation: The Gini coefficient runs from 0, perfect equality, toward 1, or 100 if expressed as a percentage, for perfect inequality. This item does not ask for a calculation.

items.topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
items.stem: A means-tested benefit, compared with a universal benefit of the same total cost,

options.A: can concentrate help on low-income households but may discourage extra earnings if the benefit is withdrawn sharply
options.C: is paid to every household regardless of income and therefore always costs less
options.D: is the same thing as a regressive tax

items.explanation: Means-testing targets the poor. A high withdrawal rate as earnings rise acts like a high marginal tax and can create a poverty trap.

items.topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
items.stem: A poverty line is

options.A: the diagonal of the Lorenz curve
options.B: the income threshold used to decide who is counted as poor

items.explanation: People below the line are classified as poor. An absolute line is a fixed real basket. A relative line is often a fraction of median income.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
items.stem: A progressive income tax is one in which

options.A: the average rate of tax rises as income rises
options.B: the average rate of tax is constant
options.C: every household pays the same number of dollars
options.D: the average rate of tax falls as income rises

items.explanation: Progressive means the average tax rate rises with income. A constant average rate is proportional. A falling average rate is regressive.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
items.stem: Absolute poverty means

options.B: a person has less income than the richest household
options.C: a person falls below a fixed minimum standard of living
options.D: income is below the national average, even if basic needs are met

items.explanation: Absolute poverty uses a fixed threshold, such as the cost of a basic basket of food, clothing and shelter. It does not depend on how rich other people are.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
items.stem: Inequality of opportunity differs from inequality of outcome because

options.B: opportunity is measured only by the terms of trade
options.C: opportunity concerns unequal access to education, jobs or assets, while outcome is the resulting income or wealth

items.explanation: Two societies can have different views about whether a gap in results is acceptable if the starting chances were equal. The syllabus distinction is between the chances people have and the incomes they end up with.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
items.stem: On a Lorenz curve, greater inequality is shown by

options.A: a curve lying on the diagonal
options.B: a curve further from the diagonal line of equality

items.explanation: The diagonal means each share of households receives the same share of income. The further the Lorenz curve bows away, the more unequal the distribution.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
items.stem: Relative poverty means

options.A: a person is below a threshold that never refers to other people
options.C: the functional share of wages is zero
options.D: a person is poor compared with the typical living standard in that society

items.explanation: Relative poverty depends on the distribution. A household can meet basic needs and still be relatively poor if its income is far below the median.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
items.stem: The functional distribution of income shows

options.A: how income is shared among wages, rent, interest and profit
options.D: how income is shared among households

items.explanation: Functional distribution classifies income by the factor that earns it. Size distribution classifies it by people or households.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
items.stem: The size distribution of income shows

options.A: how income is shared among individuals or households
options.C: only the share of profit in national income
options.D: export prices relative to import prices

items.explanation: Size distribution answers who receives income, from richest to poorest, rather than which factor earned it.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
items.stem: A minimum wage can reduce poverty among workers who keep their jobs, but it may not reduce poverty overall if

options.A: every worker's marginal product rises by the amount of the wage
options.B: the wage is set below equilibrium and does not bind
options.C: employment of low-skilled workers falls and some lose all of their wage
options.D: the labour market is in equilibrium at a wage above the minimum

items.explanation: The workers who remain employed gain. Workers who become unemployed lose wage income. The net effect on poverty is therefore not guaranteed.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
items.stem: A sales tax of 10 percent on all goods takes a larger share of a low income than of a high income, because the low-income household spends all of its income. The burden of the tax is

options.A: a poll tax, which is unrelated to spending

items.explanation: Even a flat rate on spending can be regressive if poorer households spend a larger fraction of income. The average tax rate then falls as income rises.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
items.stem: Cash transfers to low-income households are intended to

options.A: reduce poverty and narrow the size distribution of disposable income
options.B: raise the Gini coefficient on purpose

items.explanation: Transfers raise the disposable income of people at the bottom. They are a direct tool of poverty alleviation and redistribution.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
items.stem: Country A has a Gini coefficient of 0.30 and Country B has a Gini coefficient of 0.55. On this measure,

options.C: income is more unequal in B than in A
options.D: income is more unequal in A than in B

items.explanation: A higher Gini coefficient means a more unequal size distribution. No formula needs to be evaluated to rank the two figures.

items.topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
items.stem: Public spending on basic education can reduce long-run inequality by

options.C: replacing the Lorenz curve with a demand curve
options.D: raising the human capital and future earnings of children from poor households

items.explanation: Education is both a merit good and a way of widening access to better-paid work. The effect on inequality is long run, through earning power.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
items.stem: Regional policy that attracts firms to a poor parish is meant to reduce inequality by

options.A: lowering the marginal product of every worker
options.B: raising labour demand and wages or employment in that parish
options.C: replacing absolute poverty with a higher Gini coefficient on purpose
options.D: shifting the parish's labour demand to the left

items.explanation: If jobs move to the poor region, local labour demand rises. That can narrow regional income gaps, though it has a cost and may not succeed if firms do not come.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
items.stem: The share of wages in national income rises and the share of profits falls. This is a change in

options.B: the price elasticity of demand only

items.explanation: Functional distribution is the split of income among factors. A move from profit toward wages is a change in that split, even before we know how households are affected.

items.topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
items.stem: Which is a recognised cause of poverty in a labour market?

options.A: Prolonged unemployment of the household's earners
options.B: A wage equal to a high marginal revenue product for every worker
options.D: Perfect equality on the Lorenz curve

items.explanation: Households without work, or with only low-paid work, are more likely to fall below a poverty line. Equality would not itself be a cause of poverty.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
items.stem: Which outcome is possible?

options.A: A Gini coefficient of 0 means one person has all the income
options.B: The Lorenz curve lies on the diagonal when inequality is extreme
options.C: Functional distribution and size distribution are the same concept
options.D: Absolute poverty falls while relative poverty rises

items.explanation: Growth can lift people above a fixed poverty line while the gap between rich and poor widens. Absolute and relative poverty therefore need not move together.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.stem: Which policy is aimed directly at the size distribution of income?

options.B: A devaluation intended only to switch expenditure
options.C: A more progressive income tax combined with transfers

items.explanation: Tax-and-transfer policy changes disposable incomes across households. The other policies are macroeconomic instruments with different primary targets.

items.topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
items.stem: A firm hiring labour in a perfectly competitive labour market should hire extra workers while

options.A: the wage is above marginal revenue product
options.B: marginal revenue product is above the wage, and stop when they are equal

items.explanation: The wage is the marginal cost of labour to a competitive employer. Profit rises by hiring while MRP exceeds that cost.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
items.stem: A monopsony in a labour market is

options.C: a single seller of the product

items.explanation: Monopsony power is on the buying side. Monopoly power is on the selling side. A firm can have one without the other.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
items.stem: A profit-maximising monopsonist hires labour where

options.A: marginal cost of labour equals marginal revenue product, and pays the lower wage read from the supply curve
options.B: the wage equals marginal revenue product, as in perfect competition
options.C: marginal cost of labour is below the wage
options.D: employment is higher than under perfect competition

items.explanation: Because the supply of labour slopes upward, hiring one more worker raises the wage paid to all, so the marginal cost of labour is above the wage. The monopsonist equates that marginal cost with MRP and pays only the supply-curve wage, which is below MRP.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
items.stem: Economic rent is

options.B: the same as normal profit by definition in every market
options.C: payment that is only just enough to keep the factor in its current use
options.D: payment to a factor above its transfer earnings

items.explanation: Economic rent is a surplus. It can be earned by any factor whose supply is less than perfectly elastic, not only by land.

items.topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
items.stem: Marginal revenue product of labour is

options.A: marginal physical product multiplied by marginal revenue
options.C: marginal physical product multiplied by the wage

items.explanation: MRP is the extra revenue from hiring one more worker. It equals MPP times MR. Only in perfect product-market competition does MR equal price.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
items.stem: Quasi-rent is

options.B: the wage in a perfectly elastic labour market
options.C: economic rent that lasts forever on a factor in permanently fixed supply
options.D: a surplus earned in the short run by a factor whose supply is temporarily fixed

items.explanation: In the short run some factors cannot leave, so their earnings contain a temporary surplus. In the long run that surplus can be competed away. Permanent rent applies when supply stays fixed.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
items.stem: The demand curve for labour slopes downward, other things equal, because

options.A: the supply of labour is fixed
options.C: diminishing returns reduce marginal physical product as more workers are hired
options.D: transfer earnings rise with the wage automatically

items.explanation: With other factors fixed, extra workers add less output. MRP therefore falls, and the firm hires more workers only at a lower wage.

items.topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
items.stem: The demand for labour is a derived demand because

items.stem: A central Classical assumption is that

items.stem: Classical unemployment is viewed mainly as

options.A: voluntary or temporary, because flexible wages clear the labour market
options.B: the same thing as a liquidity trap
options.C: a permanent equilibrium below full employment caused by sticky wages

items.explanation: If the real wage can fall, the quantity of labour demanded rises until everyone who wants work at that wage is employed. Remaining unemployment is frictional or a choice not to work at the going wage.

items.stem: Crowding out, in a Classical full-employment setting with a fixed money supply, means

options.A: taxes automatically fall in a boom

options.C: government spending raises private investment dollar for dollar with no interest-rate effect
options.D: government borrowing raises the interest rate and reduces private investment

items.explanation: At full employment, extra public borrowing competes for funds, the interest rate rises, and private investment falls. The net rise in demand is then smaller.

items.stem: A structural budget deficit is

options.B: the part of the deficit caused only by a recession
options.D: the deficit that would remain even if the economy were at its normal level of output

items.explanation: The cyclical deficit appears because revenue falls and benefits rise in a downturn. The structural deficit is the underlying stance of the budget.

options.A: tax and benefit rules that reduce the amplitude of the business cycle without a new policy decision
options.B: discretionary changes announced in each budget
options.C: tariffs that change every week by ministerial order

items.explanation: In a boom, income-tax revenue rises and unemployment benefits fall, which withdraws spending. In a slump the opposite happens.

options.A: buying securities on the open market, which is fiscal policy
options.C: increasing transfer payments to households by a large amount
options.D: raising taxes or cutting government spending

items.explanation: Contractionary fiscal policy reduces aggregate demand. Expansion would widen an inflationary gap.

items.stem: Near full employment, a bond-financed rise in government spending is more likely to crowd out private investment if

options.A: taxes are cut by the same amount and the balanced-budget multiplier is the only effect considered, with interest rates fixed
options.B: the money supply does not rise and the interest rate increases
options.C: the economy is in a liquidity trap
options.D: there is a deep recession and idle saving

items.explanation: With little spare capacity and a fixed money supply, extra borrowing pushes up interest rates. In a liquidity trap or a deep slump, that channel is weak.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.topic: Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates
items.stem: A managed float means

options.A: the rate is reset only by the IMF each morning for every country
options.B: the rate is permanently fixed and never changes
options.C: the rate is mainly market-determined but the central bank sometimes intervenes

items.explanation: A managed, or dirty, float sits between a pure float and a hard peg.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.topic: Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates
items.stem: Devaluation is

options.A: an official increase in the value of a currency
options.C: a market-driven fall in a floating rate
options.D: an official reduction in the value of a currency under a fixed exchange rate

items.explanation: Depreciation is the market fall under floating rates. Devaluation is the policy step under a peg. Revaluation and appreciation are the upward counterparts.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.topic: Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates
items.stem: Expenditure-switching policy differs from expenditure-reducing policy because

options.B: both mean a rise in government spending
options.C: switching is a cut in the money supply only
options.D: switching tries to move spending toward home goods, while reducing tries to cut total spending and imports

items.explanation: Devaluation or depreciation, and tariffs, are switching instruments. Higher taxes or interest rates that cut absorption are reducing instruments.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.topic: Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates
items.stem: Foreign direct investment is recorded in

options.A: the current account as a good
options.C: the financial account, not the current account

items.explanation: FDI is a capital flow that buys a lasting stake. It is not an export of a good, so it is not a current-account item.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.topic: Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates
items.stem: The Marshall-Lerner condition says that a devaluation improves the current account if

options.A: the country has a fixed quantity of exports and imports that cannot change
options.C: the sum of the elasticities is less than 1
options.D: the sum of the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports is greater than 1

items.explanation: If quantities hardly respond, the fall in export prices worsens the account. Enough elasticity of demand is needed for volumes to offset that price effect.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.topic: Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates
items.stem: The current account of the balance of payments includes

options.A: trade in goods, trade in services, primary income and secondary income

items.explanation: Goods and services are the trade balance in the broad sense. Primary income covers investment income. Secondary income covers transfers. FDI belongs in the financial account.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.topic: Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates
items.stem: Under a fixed exchange rate the central bank

options.A: buys or sells foreign currency to keep the rate at the peg
options.B: lets the rate move to whatever the market sets that day
options.D: sets fiscal policy as its only tool

items.explanation: Defending a peg uses reserves. If the currency is under downward pressure, the bank sells foreign currency and buys its own.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.topic: Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates
items.stem: An appreciation of the domestic currency tends to

options.A: make imports dearer and exports cheaper
options.B: make imports cheaper and can reduce imported inflation, while making exports dearer
options.C: raise the foreign-currency price of imports

items.explanation: A stronger currency buys more foreign goods per unit. Import prices in local currency fall. Exporters find it harder to sell.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.topic: Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates
items.stem: The EC dollar depreciates under a floating rate. Exports priced in EC dollars become

options.B: cheaper in foreign currency, which can switch spending toward local goods
options.D: a reason to call the change a revaluation

items.explanation: Foreigners need fewer units of their own currency to buy the exports. That expenditure-switching effect depends on the regime being a float, so the word is depreciation, not devaluation.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.topic: Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates
items.stem: Under a floating exchange rate, a rise in demand for a country's exports tends to

options.D: leave the rate unchanged because floating rates are fixed by decree

items.explanation: Foreigners need the local currency to buy the exports, so demand for that currency rises and it appreciates if the rate floats.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.stem: A common market goes beyond a customs union by allowing

options.A: free movement of factors of production among members
options.B: each member to set a different external tariff
options.D: only free movement of goods, with labour and capital still blocked

items.explanation: Goods, services, labour and capital can move. An economic union goes further and harmonises economic policy.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.stem: A customs union is a free-trade area plus

options.C: no rules on trade with outsiders
options.D: a common currency and a single central bank, and nothing less

items.explanation: Members liberalise trade among themselves and apply the same tariff to the rest of the world.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.stem: A free-trade area removes tariffs among members and

options.A: requires free movement of labour and a common fiscal policy
options.D: lets each member keep its own tariff against non-members

items.explanation: The absence of a common external tariff is what separates a free-trade area from a customs union.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.stem: An economic union typically adds, beyond a common market,

options.A: the abolition of the common external tariff
options.B: harmonised economic policies, and sometimes a common currency

items.explanation: Policy coordination is the extra step. A monetary union, with one currency, is a deeper form.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.stem: The CARICOM Single Market and Economy is intended to

options.A: be a monetary instrument of a single parish council
options.B: set the world price of oil
options.C: deepen integration among members, including freer movement of goods, services, capital and skills
options.D: replace CARICOM with a free-trade area that keeps barriers to factor movement as its goal

items.explanation: CSME is the deepening of CARICOM beyond a simple trade preference, toward a single market. It is not itself a world-trade institution.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.stem: Trade creation in a customs union is

options.A: the replacement of higher-cost domestic production by lower-cost imports from a partner
options.C: a fall in exports to zero
options.D: the replacement of lower-cost imports from outside the union by higher-cost partner imports

items.explanation: Trade creation is a gain. Trade diversion, the shift from a cheaper non-member to a dearer member because of the common external tariff, is a possible loss.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.stem: A small member of a customs union may lose if

options.A: trade creation is the only effect and partner costs are lower
options.B: the common external tariff is zero on a good it already imported freely from the partner
options.C: it specialises according to comparative advantage inside a free-trade area with no diversion

items.explanation: The welfare effect of joining is the balance of creation and diversion, plus any scale or terms-of-trade effects. Diversion can dominate.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.stem: Before a customs union, St Brice imported cement from the cheapest world supplier. After the union it buys dearer cement from a partner because the common external tariff shuts out the world supplier. This is

options.B: a free-trade area with no external tariff

items.explanation: The union has diverted trade from a lower-cost outsider to a higher-cost insider. That is trade diversion.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.stem: Which sequence moves from shallower to deeper integration?

options.B: Common market, then a free-trade area that reintroduces internal tariffs as a deepening
options.C: Customs union, then separate external tariffs as a deepening
options.D: Free-trade area, customs union, common market, economic union

items.explanation: Each step adds a commitment: a common external tariff, then factor mobility, then policy harmonisation.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.stem: Brain drain is

options.A: the import of unskilled labour only
options.C: a surplus on the capital account
options.D: a rise in the domestic birth rate of graduates

items.explanation: When trained workers leave, the sending country loses human capital. Remittances are a partial offset, not a full replacement for the lost skills.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.stem: Economic development is broader than growth because it includes

options.A: only the rise in nominal GDP
options.B: a higher Gini coefficient by definition
options.D: improvements in living standards, such as health and education, and changes in the structure of the economy

items.explanation: A country can grow and still fail to develop if health, schooling and the quality of jobs do not improve.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.stem: Economic growth means

options.A: a more equal distribution of a fixed output
options.B: any rise in the price level
options.C: an increase in real national output over time

items.explanation: Growth is a quantity concept, usually measured by the percentage change in real GDP. It is not the same as development.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.stem: Measurable Economic Welfare, as named in this syllabus, is best understood as

options.A: the same statistic as the Gini coefficient
options.D: an adjustment of a national-income measure for welfare-relevant items such as leisure and environmental costs

items.explanation: The syllabus uses Measurable Economic Welfare for a welfare-adjusted view of national income. Students are not required to compute the adjustment.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.stem: Sustainable development means meeting present needs

options.A: only by maximising this year's nominal GDP
options.B: by using up natural resources as fast as possible
options.C: without any reference to the environment
options.D: without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs

items.explanation: The standard definition requires the path of development to be one that future generations can continue.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.stem: The Human Development Index combines indicators of

options.A: inflation, unemployment and the budget deficit only
options.B: exports, imports and the exchange rate only

items.explanation: HDI is not GDP alone. A country can rank higher in income than in human development if health or schooling lags. Calculation of the index is not required.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.stem: A country has high GDP per capita but short schooling and poor health indicators. Its HDI rank is likely to be

options.A: identical to its income rank, because HDI is GDP
options.B: undefined, because education is not in the index
options.C: improved by the poor health indicators

items.explanation: HDI averages income with health and education. Weak social indicators pull the index down relative to income alone.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.stem: Growth that destroys a coral reef used by a tourism industry may fail the test of sustainable development because

options.A: environmental costs raise Measurable Economic Welfare automatically
options.B: tourism is not part of GDP
options.C: future income from the reef is sacrificed for a present gain
options.D: any rise in real GDP is sustainable by definition

items.explanation: Sustainability asks whether the activity can continue. Damaging the natural asset that future output depends on fails that test.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.stem: Which is a source of economic growth?

options.B: A larger current-account deficit with no change in productive capacity
options.C: An increase in the capital stock or an improvement in technology
options.D: A rise in the price level with quantities unchanged

items.explanation: Growth of potential output comes from more or better factors and from technical progress, not from inflation.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
items.stem: Which is a structural feature of many small island developing states?

options.A: Perfect diversification of exports by definition
options.B: A large internal market that makes trade unimportant
options.D: A narrow export base and high exposure to hurricanes and world prices

items.explanation: Small populations, limited land, openness and natural hazards make output and export earnings volatile.
items.source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

items.module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations

items.stem: A possible benefit of globalisation for a small Caribbean economy is

options.B: the end of any need for foreign exchange

items.stem: A possible cost of globalisation for a small open economy is

options.A: greater exposure to external shocks and to footloose capital
options.B: an automatic improvement in the terms of trade every year
options.C: a smaller market for every export, by definition
options.D: the inability to import goods that the country cannot produce

items.explanation: Capital and demand can leave quickly, and a narrow export base transmits world prices into local income. Those are costs to set against the gains from trade and FDI.

items.explanation: Reciprocal agreements exchange concessions. A one-way preference does not require the beneficiary to liberalise in return.

items.stem: Comparative advantage, rather than absolute advantage, is the basis for gains from trade because

items.explanation: Absolute advantage compares output per worker. Comparative advantage compares opportunity cost. Trade can benefit both sides when those opportunity costs differ.

items.stem: Output per worker per day is: Island A produces 8 units of fish or 4 units of yams; Island B produces 6 units of fish or 6 units of yams. Comparative advantage goes to the producer with the lower opportunity cost. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Island B has a comparative advantage in fish because it has the higher opportunity cost
options.B: Opportunity cost of one unit of fish in Island A is 2 units of yams
options.C: Island A has a comparative advantage in fish because its opportunity cost is 0.5 units of yams, lower than 1
options.D: Island A has a comparative advantage in both goods

items.explanation: Opportunity cost of one fish is 0.5 yams in Island A and 1 yams in Island B. Island A has the comparative advantage in fish. Island B therefore has the comparative advantage in yams. Absolute advantage in fish belongs to Island A; absolute advantage in yams belongs to Island B. Comparative advantage does not require an absolute advantage.
items.numeric_unit: units of yams per unit of fish
